terms.gloss: a gentleman: a man of a free man’s bearing, courteous and generous
terms.grammar: phrase: līberālis, līberāle (adjective, third declension) with vir or homō
evidence: Ter. Ad. 464: neque bonī neque līberālis fūnctus officium est virī
terms.comment: Līberālis is “befitting a free man”: of conduct, noble, courteous, kind; of studies, the liberal arts; and very often “generous, open-handed” (Cic. Off. 2.56). In Plautus it can mean “handsome” (Lewis & Short). Līberāliter, like a gentleman (līberāliter ēducātus, Cic. Fin. 3.57).

terms.gloss: freeborn, of good birth; frank, worthy of a free man
evidence: Cic. Lael. 65: apertē ōdisse magis ingenuī est (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: First “native”, then “freeborn” (as a noun, a freeborn man, against a freedman, lībertīnus), and so of character, noble, upright, candid (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: a respectable man, a man of standing
terms.comment: Honestus is “honoured, respectable”, and of conduct “honourable, decent” (Lewis & Short): a gentleman by standing rather than by manners.
A man of upright character, the Greek καλὸς κἀγαθός (Lewis & Short); in Cicero’s politics bonī are also the conservatives.

phrases.latin: Quem frātrī adoptandum dedistī, neque bonī neque līberālis fūnctus officium est virī.
phrases.english: The son you gave your brother to adopt has behaved neither as a good man nor as a gentleman should.

phrases.latin: est enim nōn modo līberāle paulum nōn numquam dē suō jūre dēcēdere, sed interdum etiam frūctuōsum
phrases.english: for to give up a little of one’s rights now and then is not only gentlemanly but sometimes even profitable

sources: Lewis & Short: liberalis · Lewis & Short: ingenuus · Lewis & Short: honestus · Lewis & Short: bonus
